title: Longreads + Open Thread
gist: A weekly link roundup: Byrne Hobart argues the dollar's reserve status is caught between eroding trust (asset freezes, deficits) and rising ubiquitous use (dollar debt, stablecoins), that smart-contract platforms like Ethereum and Solana underrate network effects and sit in an awkward middle ground, and that cheaper experimentation in a medium surfaces more talent. Also covered: POW-camp economics as a model of an allocation-driven economy, Terence Tao on exposition in an era of AI 'proof abundance', and a review of Evolution in Four Dimensions.

insights.claim: Per a Foreign Affairs piece by Gordon Liao, Eswar Prasad and Tony Zhang, a reserve currency must be both trusted and ubiquitous, and the US dollar is now less trusted because of America's willingness to freeze the funds of people or countries it dislikes.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Asset-freeze risk is a structural driver of reserve diversification (gold, other stores of value) regardless of the merits of individual sanctions.
insights.quote: A reserve currency needs to be both trusted and ubiquitous.
insights.locator: In Foreign Affairs, Gordon Liao, Eswar Prasad

insights.claim: For reserve-currency status it does not matter whether US asset freezes are justified; what matters is whether bad actors prefer to store ill-gotten gains in some medium other than the dollar.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Demand for non-seizable alternatives is driven by the marginal sanctioned holder, not by public opinion on the sanctions.
insights.locator: In Foreign Affairs, Gordon Liao, Eswar Prasad

insights.claim: Chronic US deficits have a paradoxical effect on the dollar: they reduce trust by eroding purchasing power but increase ubiquity by creating more dollar-denominated debt.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Deficits do not map simply to dollar weakness; the network effect of dollar debt can offset trust erosion.
insights.locator: In Foreign Affairs, Gordon Liao, Eswar Prasad

insights.claim: Dollar stablecoins reduce the US's control over how many dollars are in circulation while cementing the dollar's role as the default medium for transactions.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Stablecoin growth is dollar-hegemony-positive on usage but erodes monetary control — a trade-off for policy watchers and stablecoin issuers.
insights.locator: In Foreign Affairs, Gordon Liao, Eswar Prasad

insights.claim: Crypto tends to overrate the importance of customization and underrate network effects, which weakens smart contracts as a bull case for Ethereum and Solana.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of programmability-driven valuations for L1s; network effects matter more than features.
insights.quote: Crypto tends to overrate how important customization is and underrate network effects
insights.locator: A Read.Haus reader asks if smart contracts are dead

insights.claim: Citing Antonio García Martínez, a crypto project whose growth strategy is giving away tokens has no idea what its customer acquisition cost is, so projects fight for share within crypto rather than facing the low ROI of acquiring non-crypto-native users.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Token-incentive-driven user growth is mostly reshuffling crypto-native users; discount it when valuing protocols.
insights.quote: if your growth strategy is to give away tokens, you have no idea what your customer acquisition cost is
insights.locator: A Read.Haus reader asks if smart contracts are dead

insights.claim: Smart contracts sit awkwardly between standardized contracts people simply opt into and customized contracts using the legal system's rails, and they need a reason users won't default to either extreme.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: The smart-contract thesis needs a concrete use case where neither standard contracts nor legal customization suffice.
insights.quote: Crypto is in the middle of those two extremes, and the middle is always a tough place to be.
insights.locator: A Read.Haus reader asks if smart contracts are dead

insights.claim: High 1970s inflation made hardcovers more expensive and riskier for first-time authors, pushing experimental literary fiction into cheap trade paperbacks — the format in which editor Gary Fisketjon's authors first published.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Cost shocks to a medium redirect where experimentation happens, and the new format can acquire prestige connotations.

insights.claim: When it gets cheaper to experiment in a medium, more people try it and some of them turn out to be great, so falling production costs expand the discovery of talent.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Apply to any medium where AI or tooling slashes production costs: expect a surge in new entrants and outlier winners.
insights.quote: when it gets cheaper to experiment in some medium, more people try it, and some of them turn out to be great at it
insights.locator: Some talents are not to be denied

insights.claim: Richard Radford's study of WWII prisoner-of-war camps shows that with uniform Red Cross rations and little productive labor, prisoners built a complex trade system with cigarettes as currency, arbitrage across cultural barriers, booms and busts.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: A clean natural experiment showing money emerges to reduce transaction costs and trade barriers create arbitrage profits.
insights.locator: Richard Radford was studying economics at Cambridge

insights.claim: The modern economy resembles a POW camp because a tiny fraction of labor-hours meets basic wants, leaving the big problems as allocation problems solved by ads, financial markets and central planning inside large organizations.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Businesses that improve allocation (ads, markets, corporate planning) capture outsized value in an economy past basic needs.
insights.locator: In a way, the modern economy is like this

themes.theme: Exposition in an AI proof-abundance era

insights.claim: Terence Tao argues mathematics should have prized exposition more, which becomes more valuable in a time of AI-driven 'proof abundance' when AI can produce mathematical results without conveying how they were found.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: As AI commoditizes results, scarce value shifts to explanation and interpretability of those results.
insights.locator: One of his fairly friendly and egalitarian views

insights.claim: The happiness of a smart person is a function of how old they are when they discover they are not the smartest person, so prodigies should be placed early in extremely high-performing peer groups.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: A talent-development heuristic relevant to hiring and building elite teams.

insights.claim: Byrne Hobart argues the claim that Medicaid subsidizes big employers like Walmart makes no sense, because it would only hold if average workers were so close to subsistence they would die without redistribution, which has not described anyone in America in the last half-century.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Discount the narrative that cuts to safety-net programs would force large low-wage employers to raise wages.

insights.claim: Evolution in Four Dimensions argues epigenetic, behavioral and symbolic variation alongside genes; epigenetic inheritance allows selection and phenotypic diversity with a fixed genome, a Lamarckian mechanism bounded by Darwinian limits.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Useful lens: fast-moving adaptation layers operate on top of slow-moving fixed substrates.
insights.locator: The book proposes that instead of the one-dimensional view

insights.claim: Non-genetic adaptations such as literacy and epigenetic switching move faster than genes but tend to describe brief periods of change, which arguably makes genes more important as the canvas for everything else.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Fast-layer change is bounded by the slow underlying substrate — a pattern also seen in tech stacks and markets.

insights.claim: Symbolic communication has compounding returns that can let a species hit escape velocity, making humanity's specific outcomes too path-dependent to predict even if the magnitude of impact was guessable.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Compounding information technologies make magnitude forecastable but specifics not — size the trend, not the winner.
insights.locator: But you can argue that, at some point
